title: Data Consistency
body:
# Data Consistency

<BurgerAnalogy text={"When two counters in our burger restaurant try to reserve the last available patty, seeing similar stock numbers is not enough. The reservation system must enforce that only one order gets it. Different displays may tolerate delayed updates, but the operation protecting this inventory rule needs appropriate coordination; the consistency requirement depends on what each part of the business promises."} />

Data consistency defines which values and ordering of updates readers may observe across copies of data. Different models offer different guarantees; consistency does not always require every replica to update simultaneously.

## The Challenge

When replicas are distributed across servers or geographical regions, updates take time to propagate. A system must choose how reads and writes behave during this delay and during failures, balancing its required guarantees against latency and availability.

<Callout type="neutral" title="Practical Example">

In an e-commerce platform, selling the last item requires coordinating inventory reservations to prevent overselling. Showing the same stock number on every screen is not enough: the operation that reserves the item must enforce the inventory rule, for example through a transaction or conditional write.

</Callout>

## Consistency Models

<Cards cols={3}>

<Card title="Strong Consistency" accent="slate">

With linearizable operations, a read observes the latest completed write in a single order consistent with real time. Replicas need not all update at the same physical instant.

</Card>

<Card title="Eventual Consistency" accent="slate">

Replicas may temporarily diverge but converge once updates stop and communication and conflict resolution complete.

</Card>

<Card title="Causal Consistency" accent="slate">

Causally related updates are observed in the same order. Independent concurrent updates need not have a single global order.

</Card>

</Cards>

## Implementation Strategies

<Cards cols={3}>

<Card title="Quorums" accent="slate">

Require a configured number of nodes to acknowledge an operation. The resulting guarantee also depends on quorum overlap, version handling, and the protocol used.

</Card>

<Card title="Vector Clocks" accent="slate">

Track causal relationships between updates to detect concurrency. A separate policy or data type is needed to resolve detected conflicts.

</Card>

<Card title="Consensus Protocols" accent="slate">

Algorithms such as Paxos or Raft let nodes agree on an ordered sequence of operations within their fault model.

</Card>

</Cards>

## Best Practices

<Cards cols={3}>

<Card title="Model Selection" accent="slate">

Choose the consistency model appropriate for each type of data and use case.

</Card>

<Card title="Monitoring" accent="slate">

Monitor replication delay and application invariants to detect inconsistencies.

</Card>

<Card title="Conflict Resolution" accent="slate">

Define explicit strategies for conflicts caused by concurrent updates.

</Card>

</Cards>
